scenes.title: Generative BI in Amazon Quick
scenes.narration: Business intelligence means analyzing data to help people make decisions. Imagine a sales manager asking, Which product categories grew this quarter? The question sounds conversational, but the answer must be grounded in an authorized dataset and its defined metrics. The course originally describes Amazon Q in QuickSight. The course's product note explains that QuickSight is now described as Amazon Quick Sight within Amazon Quick, while existing QuickSight APIs remain compatible. A generative business intelligence feature can help translate plain language into a chart, summary or analysis, but the user must still verify measures, filters and date ranges. Does growth mean revenue, orders or units sold? Is the comparison quarter over quarter or year over year? An attractive chart can mislead if it uses the wrong field. Sensitive datasets also require access controls. For a reliable answer, inspect the generated calculation and compare a few values with a trusted source report. The AI is an interface to data, not a substitute for sound data definitions.

scenes.title: EC2 instance type guidance
scenes.narration: Choosing an Amazon E C two instance type is a workload decision, not a popularity contest. E C two provides virtual compute capacity, and instance families trade off processor capability, memory, storage characteristics, network performance and cost. Consider two applications: a small web API with modest traffic and an analytics workload holding large datasets in memory. A general purpose configuration may suit the first, while a memory optimized family might better suit the second. An assistant can suggest candidates by matching requirements with instance characteristics, but the recommendation must be tested. Verify processor architecture compatibility, supported Region, quota limits, operating system support and actual performance measurements. Estimate costs using current rates rather than old memorized numbers. If a suggested instance is larger, it may improve performance while wasting money; if it is smaller, it may compromise response time. The decision check is to identify the bottleneck first: CPU, memory, storage I O or networking. Then test an appropriate size and compare measured outcomes.

scenes.title: Amazon Q Developer in chat applications
scenes.narration: An operations team may want alerts in a messaging channel instead of manually opening the AWS console every few minutes. The historical service AWS Chatbot was renamed Amazon Q Developer in chat applications in February twenty twenty five. In a common architecture, Amazon CloudWatch detects a configured alarm condition, Amazon Simple Notification Service, or S N S, sends a notification, and a configured chat channel receives the alert. Depending on the integration and granted permissions, authorized users may also access supported AWS commands. The important distinction is between receiving a notification and changing infrastructure. A channel that displays a high CPU alarm does not automatically grant every participant administrator access to E C two. Check that the SNS topic and chat channel are correctly configured and that the channel's IAM permissions follow least privilege. When an alert arrives, inspect the original CloudWatch metric and time window before deciding to act. The system should make the alert visible without creating unreviewed authority.

scenes.title: Amazon Q data integration in AWS Glue
scenes.narration: Data integration work often involves extracting records from a source, transforming fields and writing results to another destination. AWS Glue helps run data integration and extract transform load workflows. Amazon Q data integration in AWS Glue can help someone ask about a workflow, draft PySpark transformation code and investigate errors. PySpark is a Python interface for Apache Spark, a system used to process large datasets. Imagine cleaning customer rows by converting dates, removing invalid records and selecting the columns needed for an analytics job. An AI assistant might propose a PySpark script, but it does not guarantee the transformation is correct. Review schema names and sample records, handle missing values, test on small data and confirm the output before running a large job. A suggested script is not necessarily an executed change. When troubleshooting, inspect the actual error messages, job logs and data permissions. A good learning question is: what must happen after code generation? A responsible engineer reviews and tests the proposed data pipeline.
